clue.text: Rock band coming back to sing in commercial

indicators.note: coming back tells us to read the band's name from right to left

parts.note: R.E.M. was an American rock band
to chant is to sing

explanation.surface: A rock group returns to sing in a television advert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial' looks like the noun for an advert, but it is the adjective. 'Coming back' turns REM into MER.
explanation.definitionFit: Merchant used as an adjective means relating to trade, as in merchant shipping or a merchant bank.

clue.text: Field officer's first wife overcome by drink

indicators.note: in a down clue, being overcome by something means sitting below it, so the drink comes on top

parts.note: mead is an alcoholic drink made from honey

indicators.note: first asks for the opening letter of the word officer's

explanation.surface: An officer and his wife have both been drinking too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overcome by' is a placing word in a down clue: O and W go underneath MEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A meadow is a grassy field, often one kept for hay.

clue.text: Carpet salesman free to tour island

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all round it, so the word for free wraps around the island

parts.note: to rid is to free, as in rid of pests
the Isle of Man, a British crown dependency, is often clued simply as island

explanation.surface: A carpet salesman is free to travel round an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carpet' looks like a noun going with salesman, but it is the verb meaning to tell off.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is informal British usage for summoning them to be scolded, which is a rebuke or telling-off.

clue.text: Contributing to each asteroid's speed

indicators.note: Contributing to says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Something adds to the velocity of every asteroid in space.
explanation.definitionFit: Speed and haste are synonyms, both meaning swiftness of movement or action.

clue.text: Sees once it's spelt out

indicators.note: spelt out here suggests the letters are laid out afresh, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone recognises a word once it has been spelt out letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To notice something is to see or spot it, so the verb forms are synonyms.

clue.text: Tabloid editor absorbed in right to work

indicators.note: absorbed in means taken inside, so the editor goes within the letters for right

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A tabloid editor is wholly absorbed in the right to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tabloid' looks like an adjective for the editor, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Red-top is British slang for a tabloid newspaper, from the red mastheads of papers like The Sun.

clue.text: List what school leavers ought to be by the end of scheme

indicators.note: the end of asks for the final letter of the word scheme

parts.words: what school leavers ought to be
parts.note: pupils leaving school should be able to handle numbers, that is be numerate

explanation.surface: A list of what a scheme expects school leavers to achieve.
explanation.walkthrough: The end of 'scheme' gives E, which goes in front of NUMERATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To enumerate is to list items one by one, naming or counting each in turn.

clue.text: A letter of thanks after Henry's found in the middle of Cheltenham

indicators.note: after places the word for thanks at the end
found in means the letter for Henry sits inside the central letters
the middle of picks out the two central letters of the ten-letter word Cheltenham

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
ta is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: A thank-you letter from Henry turns up somewhere in Cheltenham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A letter of thanks' reads as a thank-you note, but 'A letter' is the definition, a Greek letter. H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Showing peevish irritation when a native American turned up in Bury

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the word for bury

parts.note: to plant something is to bury it in the ground

indicators.note: in a down clue turned up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: a Ute is a member of a Native American people of the western US

explanation.surface: Someone sulks when a Native American arrives in the Lancashire town of Bury.
explanation.walkthrough: Bury looks like the Lancashire town but is the verb. 'Turned up' turns UTE into ETU.
explanation.definitionFit: Petulant describes someone sulky and bad-tempered over trifles, which fits peevish irritation.

clue.text: Suitable in the circumstances to pose by river feeding a monkey

indicators.note: feeding means going into, so the river and pose go inside the monkey

parts.note: an ape is loosely a monkey
the Po is the longest river in Italy
to sit is to pose for a portrait

explanation.surface: Someone poses by a river while feeding a monkey, which seems fitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Apposite means apt or well suited to the situation, which is what suitable in the circumstances says.

clue.text: Brilliant books on fish

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the books follow the fish

parts.note: luce is an old word for a pike
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A collection of brilliant books about fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucent means shining or glowing, so it fits brilliant in its sense of bright.

clue.text: See over the highest parts

indicators.note: over in a down clue says the word is flipped, read from the bottom up

parts.note: to spot something is to see it

explanation.surface: An instruction to look over the uppermost sections of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' looks like part of 'see over' but it turns SPOT round.
explanation.definitionFit: The tops of things are their uppermost parts, their summits.

clue.text: Celebrity chef runs out of fruit

indicators.note: out means the letter for runs is removed from the chef's name

parts.note: Jamie Oliver is a well-known British TV chef
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A famous chef has run out of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs out of' reads as one phrase, but 'out' is the deletion and 'of' merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: The olive is the small oily fruit of the olive tree.

clue.text: Shut up about everyone's narrow escape

parts.note: to close a shop is to shut it up
C is short for circa, about
all means everyone; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Telling someone to shut up about a near miss everyone had.
explanation.definitionFit: A close call is an idiom for a near miss, a danger only just avoided.

clue.text: It evokes sadness in Oundle's head in a number of ways

indicators.note: the second in places the initial letter inside the word for ways

parts.note: paths are ways, and several of them make a number of ways

indicators.note: head asks for the first letter of Oundle

explanation.surface: Something brings out sorrow in the head teacher of Oundle, an English public school, in many ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oundle's head' looks like a headmaster; it is just the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathos is the quality in art or life that arouses pity or sorrow.

clue.text: Reviews that are about live TV programme

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the word for live
reviews here means looks over again, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: to be is to live or exist

explanation.surface: Critics' reviews of a live television show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reviews' rearranges THATARE into HEARTAT, which goes about BE. Heartbeat was a long-running British TV police drama set in 1960s Yorkshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartbeat is the title of a British television series, so the answer is an example of a TV programme.

clue.text: Substitute's goals finally beat Germany at home

indicators.note: finally asks for the last letter of goals

parts.note: to tan someone is to beat them
D is the international vehicle code for Germany
in means at home

explanation.surface: A substitute's late goals beat Germany in a home match.
explanation.definitionFit: A stand-in is a deputy who takes another's place, a replacement.

clue.text: This wealthy chap not quite hiding anger over court order

indicators.note: hiding means the shortened rich man's name conceals the other letters inside it
not quite means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: Dives is the rich man in the parable of Lazarus

indicators.note: in a down clue over places the anger above the court

parts.note: ire is anger

explanation.surface: A rich man barely conceals his rage at a court order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Court order' reads as one phrase, but only 'order' is the definition. Dives less S gives DIVE, which hides IRE and CT.
explanation.definitionFit: A directive is an official instruction, so it is a kind of order.

clue.text: Use new pool to unwind and relax

indicators.note: to unwind suggests the letters are untangled and laid out in a new order

explanation.surface: Use the new swimming pool to unwind and relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unwind' looks like part of the definition, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To loosen up is a phrasal idiom for becoming less tense, easing off.

clue.text: Spare dance card

parts.note: an odd item is a spare one, left over
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A spare ticket card for a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Card' looks like a dance card but means an eccentric person.
explanation.definitionFit: A card is informal for an eccentric or amusing person, as is an oddball.

clue.text: Song about heartless imp

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the shortened word is read backwards
heartless removes the central letter

parts.note: an imp is a little devil

explanation.surface: A song about a cruel little imp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heartless' looks like a description of the imp but removes V from DEVIL, leaving DEIL; 'about' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: A lied is a German art song, such as those of Schubert.

clue.text: Mystery writer to attempt verse

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe wrote early detective mysteries
to try is to attempt

explanation.surface: A mystery writer tries his hand at verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Poetry is literature written in verse form.

clue.text: Crossing pages out to cover up a bit of scandal

indicators.note: to cover up means the rearranged letters enclose the other pieces
out signals that the letters are rearranged, put out of order
a bit of asks for the first letter of scandal

explanation.surface: A newspaper tears out pages to hush up a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' rearranges PAGES into PSAGE, which covers A and S.
explanation.definitionFit: A passage is a crossing or voyage, as in a sea passage.

clue.text: Count returning after exercise gets shot

parts.note: PE is physical education, exercise

parts.note: to tell is to count, as in all told

explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a nobleman but is the verb tell, which 'returning' turns into LLET.

clue.text: Unambitious changes blocked by the French

parts.note: shifts are changes

clue.text: Helping to make Waldheim a German idol

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

clue.text: Strongbox discovered in church is French

parts.note: est is French for is

troublesome suggests the letters are thrown into disorder

clue.text: Let Maria off with stuff

clue.text: Fairly unimportant to break rule? Just the opposite

Just the opposite flips the roles, so the rule breaks into the unimportant word

parts.note: petty means trivial, unimportant

explanation.surface: Breaking a rule is fairly trivial, or is it the other way round?
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, PETTY would go inside R; 'Just the opposite' puts R inside PETTY instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretty as an adverb means fairly or moderately, as in pretty good.

clue.text: It's worn for protection when hit on bottom

indicators.note: in an across clue on puts the word for hit after the word for bottom

parts.note: seat is a polite word for the bottom
to belt is to hit hard

explanation.surface: Something worn to protect you when you are smacked on the backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests padding against a spanking; the answer is car safety equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A seat belt is a strap worn in a vehicle to protect the wearer in a crash.
